content.user_title: Turn One Idea into Twitter and LinkedIn Posts
content.value_statement: Identical posts often lack the structure each platform expects. This skill writes separate Twitter and LinkedIn drafts from one idea and explains their differences.
actual_capabilities: Restate the core idea in one plain sentence before drafting.
Draft a concise Twitter post with an opening line that works independently.
Draft a LinkedIn post with context, line breaks, and a clear lesson.
Check for misplaced platform phrasing and repeated distinctive sentences.
Deliver both posts with a brief explanation of their structural differences.
With VoiceMOAT connected, use separate platform profiles and draft scoring, plus publishing or scheduling with individual previews and approvals.
limitations: Designed for paired Twitter and LinkedIn posts, not single-platform writing.
An unclear source idea requires clarification before useful drafts can be written.
VoiceMOAT profiles, scoring, publishing, and scheduling require a connected service with a Pro or Enterprise plan.
The skill contains writing instructions, not connector code or automated platform-limit validation.

use_cases.title: Share a product lesson
use_cases.description: Turn one product lesson into a concise Twitter statement and a contextual LinkedIn post.

use_cases.title: Explain a technical insight
use_cases.description: Present a technical insight differently for Twitter readers and LinkedIn professionals without changing the central claim.

use_cases.title: Prepare paired client drafts
use_cases.description: Create distinct drafts for both platforms and explain the structural choices during client review.

prompt_templates.title: Draft a simple post pair
prompt_templates.prompt: Write separate Twitter and LinkedIn posts about [idea]. State the core idea first, then give both drafts and one sentence explaining their differences.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: start with a clear idea.

prompt_templates.title: Extract an idea from existing text
prompt_templates.prompt: Use [source text] to identify one core idea. Ask for clarification if needed, then write independent Twitter and LinkedIn drafts and explain the differences.

prompt_templates.title: Review and rewrite a post pair
prompt_templates.prompt: Review [Twitter draft] and [LinkedIn draft] for misplaced platform phrasing and repeated sentences. Rewrite both from their shared idea and explain the structural changes.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: improve drafts that sound too similar.

prompt_templates.title: Use connected platform profiles
prompt_templates.prompt: With VoiceMOAT connected, draft both posts about [idea] using each platform profile and score each draft. Preview separately; request approval before scheduling each.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: prepare profile-based drafts with separate scheduling approvals.

output_examples.input: Create Twitter and LinkedIn posts about testing a signup form before rebuilding the whole website.
output: Core idea: Test the signup form before committing to a full website rebuild.
Twitter: Before rebuilding your website, test the signup form. A smaller experiment can tell you where the real problem is.
LinkedIn: A website redesign is a large commitment. Testing the signup form first can reveal whether the problem needs a smaller change.
Difference: Twitter leads with the recommendation; LinkedIn introduces the decision and its context.

output_examples.input: Write both posts about recording the reasons behind team decisions.
output: Core idea: Record why a team made a decision, not just what it decided.
Twitter: A decision log needs the reason, not just the result. Future teammates will need to understand what you were solving.

LinkedIn: When a team records a decision, the outcome is only part of the story.

Include the constraints and alternatives behind it.

That context helps future teammates understand the choice before revisiting it.
Difference: Twitter compresses the lesson; LinkedIn adds practical context and separates the supporting points.

best_practices: Confirm the central idea in plain language before writing either post.
Write each draft independently and check for phrasing that belongs to the other platform.
Review both drafts for accuracy and approve each post separately when using connected publishing tools.
anti_patterns: Copying identical wording to both platforms and changing only the length.
Drafting from an unclear paragraph without identifying its main point.
Treating approval for one platform as permission to publish on both.

faq.question: What does this skill produce?
faq.answer: It produces a core idea, separate Twitter and LinkedIn drafts, and a short explanation of the differences.

faq.question: Can I provide an existing post?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill extracts the underlying idea and writes both versions independently instead of copying the original wording.

faq.question: Can I use it for only one platform?
faq.answer: That is outside its intended scope. The workflow is designed to produce both Twitter and LinkedIn posts.

faq.question: Do I need VoiceMOAT to draft posts?
faq.answer: No. The core drafting workflow works without VoiceMOAT; platform profiles, scoring, publishing, and scheduling depend on the connector.

faq.question: What does the VoiceMOAT connector require?
faq.answer: The skill states that the connector requires a VoiceMOAT Pro or Enterprise plan.

faq.question: Will both posts publish automatically?
faq.answer: No. The connected workflow specifies a separate preview and one-time confirmation for each post.
